newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians treat king to rousing welcome in village.
newsitem.headline: Albanians treat king to rousing welcome in village.

text.p: Albania's long-exiled King Leka launched a campaign to restore the monarchy in the violence-stricken Balkan nation on Sunday with a triumphant journey to his ancestral village.

Greeted by enormous crowds of cheering supporters, he said in his first speech to the public since returning from abroad last weekend that it was time for Albanians to put down their guns and work together for peace and order.
"Peace, brotherhood and unity -- not fratricide," said Leka, who was two days old when his father King Zog fled the country before invading Italian fascists 58 years ago.
More than 5,000 cheering people came to the dusty mountain village of Burgajet, the birthplace of Zog, a tribal chieftain who became president in 1922 and proclaimed himself king in 1928.
Waving red-and-black Albanian flags, many villagers greeted the king by firing automatic rifles wildly into the clear blue sky.
The king silently shed a tear as he placed flowers at his grandmother's grave in the town he had never before seen.

"I am very happy to be with my family again," said the king upon arriving in Burgajet, a farming village known for its sheep 120 km (70 miles) north of Tirana. "I will travel across the country to spread the message of peace and unity."

Albanian President Sali Berisha has promised the king a referendum on the monarchy. Even though the timing was left open, Leka said he was delighted and plans to visit towns and villages north and south before the referendum.
About 300 people have been killed and more than 700 injured in the anarchy that erupted after fraudulent investment schemes wiped out the savings of many Albanians.
King Leka said he can help restore order and unify Albania.
"The future of Albania is in your hands," Leka told the frenzied crowd in remarks kicking off the campaign. "You will decide the future of the country, the future of its children."
His father King Zog was a powerful figure who overcame tribal, regional and secular rivalries before he fled with his family. He was barred by post-war communist leaders and died in 1961 in Paris.
Many elderly Albanians recall fondly Zog's improvements in education and infrastructure. Schools and banks were opened, roads built, police organised.
His son maintains he is the legal leader of Albania based on a constitution adopted in 1928.
In his first week back, Leka met both Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and his rival head of state, Berisha.
"I hope that you will be a factor for peace," Fino said.
King Leka, who towers over most Albanians at 2.04 metres (six feet eight inches), has been welcomed by adoring crowds.
He tried to return to Albania in 1993 but was unceremoniously tossed out within hours after his passport, marked "Kingdom of Albania", was declared invalid.

More troops in a 6,000-strong eight-nation force arrived in Albania on Sunday, bringing to about 3,500 the number of soldiers from Italy, France, Greece, Spain and Turkey now in Albania. Romania, Denmark and Austria will also send soldiers.
"It seems to be calm right now, but with so many weapons out there, it is still a dangerous country," said Captain Pierre Schill, spokesman for the French armed forces.

In Vlore, 32-year-old Ferdinand Beqo was killed by a friend with a Kalashnikov rifle during an argument in a bar on Saturday night. In a separate incident, a truck driver was killed when he was ambushed by gunmen near Gjirokaster.
The political situation in Tirana remained tense on Sunday as a spokesman for President Berisha criticised Fino for firing deputy interior minister Agim Shehu on Saturday.
In a statement published on state-run ATA news agency, the spokesman said the dismissal was not legal.

"We cannot help thinking with regret that it forms a dangerous precedent that seriously damages the relations between the constitutional institutions and their ability to function," the statement said.
